newsitem.title: UK: French bombing suspects lose extradition appeal.
newsitem.headline: French bombing suspects lose extradition appeal.

text.p: Two men accused of helping plot a wave of bombings that terrorised France in 1995 lost an appeal in the British High Court on Wednesday against extradition to Paris.

Algerian Rachid Ramda and Mustapha Boutarfa, who has dual French and Algerian nationality, had appealed against extradition on the grounds that they would not get a fair trial in "anti-Moslem" France.
The two judges at Wednesday's hearing ruled there was no evidence that French courts would be biased.
"I do not find a risk of any lack of fairness at the trial or trials of either of the applicants," Judge Sir Malcolm Pill told the court.
Both men now have 14 days to appeal to Britain's highest court, the House of Lords, against their extradition.
Ramda, 27, is wanted in France to face 23 charges in connection with bombings in Paris, Lille and Lyon in which seven people died and 170 were injured.
Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed responsibility for the attacks.
The French press described Ramda as the man who organised the financing of the bombings. He was arrested in London in November 1995 under Britain's Prevention of Terrorism Act.

His extradition to France was ordered by British magistrates a year ago, but he has been fighting the case ever since while being held in Belmarsh, the top security prison in east London designed to hold prisoners of the Irish republican guerrilla group IRA.
Boutarfa, 22, was arrested in London in March 1996 and has also been held at Belmarsh.

The men's lawyers had argued that it would be impossible for them to receive a fair trial in France because of the antagonism there to Islamic fundamentalists and press reports that have named the men and linked them to the bombings.
Former French justice minister Jacques Toubon publicly described Ramda as playing an "essential" role in the bombing campaign, Ramda's lawyers said.
Judge Pill rejected the suggestion that this would influence the judges of France's Cour d'Assises Speciale court.
"There is no serious possibility, in my judgment, that in performing their duties, they would be influenced by inflammatory press reports or the remarks of Monsieur Toubon," Pill said.
Ramda's lawyers say he had been in Britain for three years before his arrest and had been seeking asylum here.
London is home to numerous exile groups and opposition activists from around the world, many of them attracted here because refugees do not have to cease their political activities to seek asylum.
Critics have accused Britain of harbouring terrorists and troublemakers.
